stories.text: The Royalists of Newark raided again and again. Sir Charles Lucas broke into the town in January 1644 and tried to set it on fire, and in April 1645 a party from Newark took the fort at Trent Bridge. Each time Hutchinson won back what was lost, and each demand that he surrender the castle he answered with fresh defiance.

In 1947 the Trent flooded 3,000 properties, 86 factories and 28 miles of road in Nottingham, and the city's first flood defence was built that year. Photographs of West Bridgford under water are in Inspire Picture Archive. A new defence along 27 km of the river, from Sawley to Colwick, was finished in 2012.

stories.text: The medieval bridge had a chapel of St James at one end and was kept by a religious house, until on 21 February 1551 a royal charter passed its repair to the Corporation, with lands to pay for it, the Bridge Estate. Floods damaged it again and again, and in 1683 they swept away its northern half. Rebuilt with fifteen arches, 538 ft long in all, it stood until its foundations grew unsafe, and in the 1860s a new bridge was begun.

In 1156 a stone bridge of more than 20 arches was begun here. It was known as the Hethbeth bridge, and two of its arches survive on the south bank. The present iron bridge nearby was designed by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, built between 1868 and 1871, and widened to 80 feet in 1924–26.

Marriott Ogle Tarbotton was Nottingham's Borough Engineer from 1859. He designed Trent Bridge, planned the town's underground sewers, culverted the River Leen and built the viaduct over the railway on Carrington Street in 1866.

303808.sum: Trent Bridge is an iron and stone road bridge across the River Trent in Nottingham, England. It is the principal river crossing for entrance to the city from the south, although the upstream Clifton Bridge is both larger and busier.

stories.text: The inn stood by the bridge before any cricket was played here. The cricketer William Clarke married its landlady, Mary Chapman, and in 1838 they had the field behind it cleared and fenced for the first match on what became Trent Bridge. Clarke left for London in 1845, and his stepson John Chapman ran the pub and the ground. After the First World War the Musters family, who owned both, sold them to the cricket club.

stories.text: A medieval church stood here, though little of it remains; it keeps a screen from the late 14th century. Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1872, and in 1896 a new nave and chancel were begun, their foundation stone laid by Lady Byron of Thrumpton Hall.
